fields.expected: Yes, though at pilot rather than mass scale. I built ClarityAtlas, an iOS health app, end to end in Swift and SwiftUI with Supabase, including a passive sleep-estimation system from HealthKit and Core Motion data and a "Sleep Twins" backend service that matched users on standardized behavioral features with weighted distance. It shipped into a live Johns Hopkins pilot with 30+ users. Earlier, I founded and built SnapSort, an AI photo-sorting product on Flask and AWS with a multi-model inference pipeline, and grew it past 300 users while owning pricing, positioning, and go-to-market.

fields.expected: A few. I was lead model developer on a Gates Foundation funded Johns Hopkins / South African Medical Research Council health equity project, where I trained XGBoost models on a national survey dataset of roughly 10 million records, used SHAP for feature selection and interpretation, and designed G-formula causal simulations to estimate counterfactual intervention outcomes. Separately, my independent research on Valley Fever became a sole-author publication in the Journal of Student Research and made me a national finalist at the Junior Science and Humanities Symposium, after I built an SIR model from its differential equations and programmed a microcontroller dust sensor in C/C++. On the product side, my cofounders and I got ClarityAtlas in front of the Johns Hopkins president by knocking on the door of Garland Hall during Lighting of the Quads, which turned into a formal meeting months later and a non-binding investment indication of about $75,000 for roughly 7 to 8 percent.
